name: Kinematic Video and Generated Movement
title: Kinematic Video and Generated Movement
answer: Kinematic video and generated movement covers systems that record, analyse, and synthesise human or animal motion for choreography, animation, and performance. It sits between motion capture, dance notation, and generative video, treating a body's changing joint positions as a sequence that can be learned and replayed. The field includes generating new dance phrases from text or music, transferring motion between different body types, and producing video where the movement, not just the background, is synthetic. Practitioners use it to prototype choreography, extend archival recordings, and build interactive installations.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on motion capture data, usually skeletal keypoint sequences recorded at high frame rates, alongside ordinary video for appearance. Training and inference typically require GPU clusters for video diffusion models, while real-time use may run on a single workstation with a pose estimation model and a lightweight generator. Storage and retrieval depend on motion libraries organised by joint hierarchy, timing, and style tags. Many pipelines separate the motion representation from the rendered body, so the same movement can drive different avatars or camera angles.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common approach is to train a generative model on paired examples of motion and text, music, or still poses, then sample new sequences that match a prompt. Pose estimation first converts source video into keypoints, and a motion model learns the transitions between those keypoints over time. Some systems use latent diffusion on short motion clips, while others use autoregressive prediction of joint rotations. Choreographers often intervene by editing the generated keypoints, applying constraints such as balance or contact with the floor, and then rendering the result with a separate video model.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions centre on who owns a generated movement phrase and whether training on a dancer's recorded performance requires consent beyond the original recording contract. Risks include replicating a performer's signature style without credit, using motion data from culturally specific dance forms without permission, and creating synthetic video that misattributes movement to a real person. Provenance practice is still forming, but many projects now record the source motion capture, the model version, and the human edits alongside any output. This is a description of current practice, not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward real-time co-creation, where a dancer's live movement is extended or answered by a generative model with low enough latency for stage use. Better physical plausibility, such as foot contact and weight shift, is a near-term goal, as is finer control over style and emotional tone. Motion synthesis is also becoming more accessible through browser-based tools that do not require a motion capture studio. Over time, generated movement may become a standard part of rehearsal and previsualisation, with clearer norms around credit and consent.
